title: Lululemon founder makes 'egregious' remarks about women at Calgary leadership forum
summary: CBC News has confirmed with two attendees that Chip Wilson's comments included that women aren't having as many children as men want, that birth control is crucial to women's professional development…

image.caption: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson is shown in Vancouver in September 2022. Wilson is under fire for comments he made at a women's leadership forum in Calgary on Monday. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

CBC News has confirmed with two attendees that Chip Wilson's comments included that women aren't having as many children as men want, that birth control is crucial to women's professional development and that the top female brands are run by men because men know what looks good on women's bodies.
Chip Wilson's comments include that men know what looks good on women's bodies
It was meant to be an intimate chat about entrepreneurship with the founder of Lululemon.

Instead, Chip Wilson is under fire for his "egregious" comments about women's bodies and reproductive choices, which reportedly included his assertions that men are importing brides from Thailand to have their children.

"It sounds like you’re painting a future reminiscent of The Handmaid’s Tale," Nuvyn Peters, the CEO of non-profit Axis Connects, told Wilson during the fireside chat on Monday at the Axis Connects Leadership Forum in Calgary, referring to Margaret Atwood's 1985 dystopian novel.

More than 700 business leaders attended the women's forum, where some of the speakers included former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, Olympic ice dancing gold medallist Tessa Virtue, musician Jann Arden and Wilson — the billionnaire founder of Lululemon Athletica who stepped down as company CEO in 2013.
Wilson's talk does not appear to be posted anywhere online. But CBC News has confirmed with two attendees at the forum that his comments, first reported by the Globe and Mail, are correct.
A screengrab of an Instagram post by Axis Connects from Oct. 1 advertises Lululemon founder Chip Wilson as a speaker at its Nov. 23 leadership forum in Calgary. (@axisconnects/Instagram)

They include that women aren't having as many children as men want, that birth control is crucial to women's professional development and that the top female brands are run by men because men know what looks good on women's bodies.

Wilson, 71, who was born in Los Angeles and has dual American-Canadian citizenship, also said that men are resorting to importing brides from other countries like Thailand, according to the attendees who spoke with CBC News.
Calgary career coach Madeleine Natale was at Monday's event and described Wilson's comments as "egregious."

"Coming on the heels of the empowering talk by Jann Arden, it felt like the wind was knocked right out of my sails," Natale said. "In this day and age, attention is one of the most precious gifts we can give. It didn't take me long to realize that my attention was not a gift I wanted to give during that talk."
'Concern and disappointment'

Wilson's event at the women-focused leadership forum was advertised online as an "intimate fireside chat" and an "honest conversation about how a serial entrepreneur thinks, builds, struggles and keeps moving forward."

CBC News reached out to Wilson but has not yet heard back. But a spokesperson for him told the Globe and Mail earlier this week, "This is an effort to discount Chip Wilson’s record of mentoring women who have become executives and entrepreneurs in their own right to drive revenue with a clickbait headline."

items: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson says pants 'don't work' for some bodies

blocks.text: It's not Wilson's first controversy. He stepped down as Lululemon CEO in 2013 during the fallout from his comments that seemed to blame people's bodies for an issue the company was having with its pants being too sheer. That year, the company had recalled nearly one-fifth of its pants because of the problem.
"Quite frankly, some women's bodies just actually don't work for it," Wilson said in a Bloomberg TV interview. "It's really about the rubbing through the thighs, how much pressure is there."
A Lululemon store is shown in Toronto in November 2025. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

Wilson, who remains one of Lululemon's top shareholders, also came under fire in 2024 for comments blasting the company's inclusion and diversity efforts, in which he objected to the company's use of models with a range of body types.
Axis Connects, a non-profit that works to advance women in business leadership roles, said Wilson's comments on Monday don't align with its values.

"We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the leadership forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects," the organization said in a statement to CBC News.
"We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community."

items: Lululemon founder faces backlash for blasting company's diversity, inclusion efforts

blocks.text: Natale, the career coach, said she's "very disappointed" by what she heard Wilson say on Monday, but she also wants the conversation to move on from one person's voice.
"I am choosing not to give these words any more of my energy than that," she said.

She lamented that Wilson's comments have received so much attention, "when so many other women's voices from the conference should be amplified." Arden, for instance, spoke about adapting to change and "held everyone's rapt attention," Natale said.
"This is a moment in time where we can all think a little more deeply about the challenges women continue to face in leadership."

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss.
